notes.meaning: Satan uses a shrewd serpent to approach the woman with a crafty question. He twists God's generous words to make God seem harsh and stingy, suggesting that God had forbidden every tree in the garden.

The woman answers the serpent by explaining that they are allowed to eat from almost all the garden trees. However, she softens God's certain warning of death and adds a rule of her own about not even touching the fruit, which gave Satan an opening.
The serpent directly contradicts God's warning by telling the woman she will not die. He tries to convince her that God made an empty threat and that sin has no real penalty.
The tempter claims that God is jealously keeping back something good from humans. He promises that eating the fruit will open their eyes and make them like God, deciding good and evil for themselves.
The woman looks at the tree, desires its fruit for food and wisdom, and disobeys God by eating it. She then gives some to her husband, who was with her, and he eats it as well.
Immediately after eating, the couple's eyes are opened to their own guilt and shame. Realizing they are naked, they sew fig leaves together to make coverings, trying in vain to hide their condition.

In the cool breeze of the day, Adam and his wife hear the sound of the Lord God approaching in the garden. Driven by a guilty conscience and fear of God, they hide among the trees instead of coming to meet Him.
The Lord God calls out to the man and asks where he is. God is not looking for information, but graciously reaches out to lead Adam to face his sin and confess it.
Adam replies that he heard God's voice and hid because he was afraid and naked. He admits his fear and shame, but tries to avoid talking about his actual disobedience.

God asks Adam how he became aware of his nakedness and whether he ate from the forbidden tree. God uses these questions to pierce Adam's conscience and help him see that his shame came from breaking God's law.
Adam confesses that he ate the fruit, but he immediately shifts the blame to his wife and to God for creating her. Fallen human nature quickly tries to excuse its own guilt by accusing others.
The Lord God asks the woman what she has done. Following her husband's pattern, she avoids taking full responsibility by blaming the serpent for deceiving her.
God pronounces judgment on the serpent without asking it any questions, cursing it below all animals. It is sentenced to crawl on its belly and eat dust, picturing total humiliation and defeat.

God declares lasting warfare between the serpent and the woman, and between their descendants. The woman's promised descendant will suffer a struck heel but will deliver a fatal blow by crushing the serpent's head, pointing forward to Christ's victory over the devil.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition has often read 'she will crush your head' based on older Latin texts, seeing Mary as the New Eve who shares in defeating the devil through her Son Jesus.

notes.meaning: God tells the woman that she will experience greatly increased pain during pregnancy and childbirth. Sin also damages marriage, bringing relational struggle and tension into the husband and wife relationship.

differ.view: Many evangelicals view the woman's desire as a natural longing and devotion that is placed under her husband's authority.
Some evangelicals believe the woman's desire refers to a urge to challenge or control her husband, leading to ongoing conflict.

notes.meaning: Because Adam listened to his wife instead of obeying God, God curses the ground on his account. Getting food will no longer be easy, but will require hard, painful labor throughout his life.
The cursed earth will now produce troublesome thorns and weeds that fight against human farming. Instead of eating luscious garden fruit, Adam must work hard to grow crops in the open fields.
Adam will have to labor with sweaty effort to earn his daily bread until physical death ends his work. Because he was formed from the earth, his body will return to the dust when he dies.

Adam gives his wife the name Eve, which means life, because she would become the mother of all human beings. Even under the sentence of death, Adam shows faith in God's promise that human life and the promised Savior would continue through her.

The Lord God graciously replaces their flimsy fig leaves by making durable garments out of animal skins to clothe them. This shedding of animal blood provided a covering for their shame and pointed forward to sacrifice for sin.

God observes that man has grasped an independent knowledge of good and evil through rebellion. To keep fallen humans from eating of the tree of life and living forever trapped in their sinful, broken state, God decides to remove them.
The Lord God sends Adam out of the garden of Eden to work the soil outside. While man lost his peaceful home, God mercifully sent him to a place of honest labor rather than destroying him completely.

God drives man out and places angelic guardians called cherubim and a flashing, flaming sword on the east side of Eden. This closed off access to the tree of life, reminding humanity that sinners cannot enter God's holy presence on their own.
